Note that the optimal way to remove the boards is to remove a consecutive $$$w-1$$$ boards and then leave one. Thus, every $$$w$$$-th board will remain. Therefore, the answer is $$$\displaystyle n - \left\lfloor \frac{n}{w} \right\rfloor$$$.
2194B - Offshores

Let us assume we want to make the $$$i$$$-th element the maximum. We will calculate $$$S_i = \sum\limits_{j = 1 \dots n}^{j \neq i} \lfloor \frac{a_j}{x} \rfloor$$$. Notice that the maximum number of transfers we can make to the $$$i$$$-th account from all the others is exactly this amount (since the condition $$$y \le x$$$ holds, if we make a transfer from some account $$$u$$$ to some account $$$v$$$, then $$$\lfloor \frac{a_u}{x} \rfloor$$$ will decrease by exactly $$$1$$$, while $$$\lfloor \frac{a_v}{x} \rfloor$$$ will increase by at most $$$1$$$, so intermediate transfers between accounts will not help increase $$$S_i$$$). Thus, the problem reduces to learning how to quickly compute $$$S_i$$$ for each $$$i$$$. To do this, we can calculate $$$S_{all} = \sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n} \lfloor \frac{a_j}{x} \rfloor$$$, then $$$S_i = S_{all} - \lfloor \frac{a_i}{x} \rfloor$$$
2194C - Secret message

Let's iterate over $$$d$$$ (divisor of $$$n$$$) and check if we can obtain a string with informativeness $$$d$$$. For this, for each $$$1 \leq i \leq d$$$, we need to check that there is a common letter at positions $$$i, i+d, i+2d, \dots$$$. To do this, we will iterate over the letter at position $$$i$$$ and check that this letter is also present at positions $$$i+d, i+2d, \dots$$$. For position $$$i$$$, the check can be done in $$$O\left(\frac{n}{d} \cdot k^2\right)$$$, and for all $$$i$$$, it will work in $$$O(n k^2)$$$. In total, across all $$$d$$$, the algorithm will run in $$$O(n \cdot d(n) \cdot k^2)$$$ (where $$$d(n)$$$ is the number of divisors of the number $$$n$$$, which does not exceed $$$100$$$ in the problem constraints). With careful implementation, such a solution can pass all tests, but it can be improved.

The idea: instead of storing $$$k$$$ letters at each position, let's store an array of length 26, where for each letter it is recorded whether it is present at this position or not. Now, for each $$$i$$$, we can check in $$$O\left(26 \cdot \frac{n}{d}\right)$$$ whether there is a common letter at positions $$$i, i+d, i+2d, \cdots$$$ (iterate over one of the letters at position $$$i$$$ and check that it fits for $$$\frac{n}{d}$$$). Thus, the overall asymptotic complexity of the algorithm will be $$$O(26 \cdot n \cdot d(n))$$$.
2194D - Table Cut

Let there be $$$k$$$ ones in the table. Then the maximum possible product is $$$\displaystyle \left\lfloor \frac{k}{2} \right\rfloor \cdot \left( k - \left\lfloor \frac{k}{2} \right\rfloor \right)$$$. We will show that the answer is always achievable. We want to separate the part with $$$\displaystyle x = \left\lfloor \frac{k}{2} \right\rfloor$$$. We will find the last row such that the sum of ones in the prefix of the rows is $$$\leq x$$$.
In the next row, we will take the necessary number of elements from the suffix so that the sum above becomes equal to $$$x$$$.
After that, the cut is restored from the figure above.
2194E - The Turtle Strikes Back

Let us start with a basic solution. First, consider some path with the maximum total enjoyment from $$$(1, 1)$$$ to $$$(n, m)$$$. Observe that Raphael must block one of the cells on this path. For each cell that Raphael may block, we can independently compute the maximum enjoyment that Michelangelo can obtain by moving from $$$(1, 1)$$$ to $$$(n, m)$$$ while avoiding this cell. This approach is naturally implemented using standard grid dynamic programming and leads to a time complexity of $$$O(nm(n + m))$$$.

To further optimize the solution, fix one of the maximum-enjoyment paths $$$S$$$ from $$$(1, 1)$$$ to $$$(n, m)$$$ on the original grid. Denote the cells of this path by $$$s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n + m - 1}$$$. Observe that if Raphael does not block any of these cells, Michelangelo can follow the path $$$S$$$ and obtain the maximum possible enjoyment. Therefore, an optimal move for Raphael always consists of blocking some cell $$$s_k$$$.
Let us consider what happens when the cell $$$(i, j) = s_k$$$ is blocked. Michelangelo has two options:
follow the same path $$$S$$$, losing exactly $$$2 a_{i,j}$$$ enjoyment, which results in the value $$$maxS - 2 a_{i,j}$$$;
choose a path from $$$(1, 1)$$$ to $$$(n, m)$$$ that does not pass through the cell $$$(i, j)$$$.
The first option can be computed directly. The second requires determining the maximum enjoyment of a path that bypasses the blocked cell.

Observe that a path does not pass through the cell $$$(i, j)$$$ if and only if it contains some cell $$$(a, b)$$$ such that either $$$a \lt i$$$ and $$$b \gt j$$$, or $$$a \gt i$$$ and $$$b \lt j$$$. This allows us to consider all such cells $$$(a, b)$$$ as possible bypass points.
We introduce two auxiliary dynamic programming tables:
$$$dpS[x][y]$$$ — the maximum enjoyment on a path from $$$(1, 1)$$$ to $$$(x, y)$$$;
$$$dpT[x][y]$$$ — the maximum enjoyment on a path from $$$(x, y)$$$ to $$$(n, m)$$$.
Then the contribution of a path passing through the cell $$$(a, b)$$$ is equal to $$$dpS[a][b] + dpT[a][b] - a[a][b]$$$.

For each cell $$$s_k$$$, we store the maximum of this value over all valid bypass points and denote it by $$$dp[k]$$$. The final answer is then given by $$$\min_k \left( \max\bigl(dp[k],\; maxS - 2 a[s_k]\bigr) \right)$$$.

It remains to optimize the computation of the values $$$dp[k]$$$. For a fixed cell $$$(i, j)$$$, it is sufficient to consider only the cells $$$(i + 1, q \lt j)$$$ and $$$(p \lt i, j + 1)$$$. For these cells, we need to quickly find the maximum value of the expression $$$dpS[x][y] + dpT[x][y] - a[x][y]$$$.

Note that such maxima are queried over prefixes of rows and columns, so they can be precomputed in $$$O(nm)$$$. After that, for each cell $$$(i, j)$$$, the value of the best bypassing path can be obtained in $$$O(1)$$$ time.
Thus, the final solution runs in $$$O(nm)$$$ time and uses $$$O(nm)$$$ memory.
2194F2 - Again Trees... (hard version)

Let $$$dp[v][x]$$$ be the number of ways to select a set of edges from the subtree of this vertex, including the edge from vertex $$$v$$$ to its ancestor, such that the XOR of the cut-off vertices in the subtree (vertices which is not connected to $$$v$$$ now) equals $$$x$$$. To recompute $$$dp$$$, we first need to calculate the XOR convolution of the $$$dp$$$ values of the children. The XOR convolution of arrays $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ of length $$$2^k$$$ is an array $$$c_i = \sum a_j \times b_{j \oplus i}$$$. For now, we will compute it in $$$O(len(a) \times len(b))$$$. After performing the XOR convolution for all children, we must process the option of removing the edge from $$$v$$$ to its ancestor. For this, we iterate over $$$x$$$, and if xor_subtree[$$$v$$$] $$$\oplus$$$ $$$x \in b$$$, then we need to add $$$dp[v][x]$$$ to $$$dp[v][0]$$$. Thus, this solution works in $$$O(n \times 2^{30} \times 2^{30})$$$, since $$$0 \leq x \lt 2^{30}$$$, and naive convolution works in $$$O(len(a) \times len(b))$$$. Of course, we are not satisfied with this time complexity, but note that $$$x$$$ in this $$$dp$$$ is an XOR combination of the set $$$b$$$.

Let's choose a basis from the set $$$b$$$ and store $$$dp$$$ in this basis. Now, the number of possible $$$x$$$ in $$$dp$$$ is $$$2^k$$$, and naive XOR convolution works in $$$4^k$$$, so the solution runs in $$$O(n \times 4^{k})$$$, which is sufficient to pass F1. There are also several other approaches for solving F1, but they cannot be optimized to solve F2.

The first optimization that improves the complexity is to perform XOR convolution using the Hadamard transform (FWHT). Then, the complexity becomes $$$O(n \times 2^k \times k)$$$, but this is still insufficient to pass F2.

We want to get rid of the multiplication by $$$k$$$. One XOR convolution via Hadamard looks like this: compute the Hadamard transform of both arrays, then compute the element-wise multiplication, and finally apply the inverse Hadamard transform. Instead of storing $$$dp[v][x]$$$, let's store $$$hadamard(dp[v][x])$$$, i.e., the Hadamard transform. Its formula is: $$$hadamard(a)[i] = \sum a_j \times (-1)^{popcount(i \ AND \ j)}$$$. Then, convolution is performed in $$$O(2^k)$$$ via element-wise multiplication. Now, the difficulty arises with the second recomputation step, where we wanted to compute the value $$$dp[v][x]$$$ at certain points $$$x$$$ and add it to $$$dp[v][0]$$$.

Let's start with the first step. We need to compute $$$\sum dp[v][b_i \oplus$$$ xor_subtree[v]$$$]$$$. It is worth noting that if xor_subtree[$$$v$$$] cannot be expressed in the basis, then such recomputation is unnecessary. First, let's compute this sum assuming xor_subtree[v] = 0. Let $$$p$$$ be an array of size $$$2^k$$$, where the positions corresponding to $$$b_i$$$ are set to 1, and all others are zeros. Then, the sum we need to compute is the zero element of the XOR convolution of $$$dp[v]$$$ and $$$p$$$. We cannot compute the convolution of $$$dp[v]$$$ and $$$p$$$ directly, but we can compute $$$q = hadamard($$$convolution of $$$dp[v]$$$ and $$$p$$$), since this is the element-wise product of $$$hadamard(dp[v])$$$ and $$$hadamard(p)$$$, and $$$hadamard(p)$$$ can be computed once at the beginning of the program. Now, we are interested in the zero element of the inverse transform of $$$q$$$, which is simply $$$(\sum q_i) / 2^k$$$. Now, recall that we have xor_subtree[$$$v$$$], but to account for it, it is enough to include in the convolution of $$$dp[v]$$$ and $$$p$$$ an array where only the position xor_subtree[$$$v$$$] is set to one. The $$$hadamard$$$ of such an array can be computed in $$$O(2^k)$$$ by definition. Thus, we have computed the required sum in $$$O(2^k)$$$.

Now, we need to compute the new $$$hadamard(dp[v])$$$ after adding the computed sum to $$$dp[v][0]$$$. But by the definition of the Hadamard transform, we can find the coefficients with which the added sum contributes to the old value of $$$hadamard(dp[v])$$$.

Thus, in this solution, the Hadamard transform needs to be explicitly computed only for calculating $$$hadamard(p)$$$, while in the rest, we explicitly compute the necessary coefficients by definition and obtain a solution in $$$O(n \times 2^k + t \times 2^k \times k)$$$, where the second term comes from computing $$$hadamard(p)$$$ for each test dataset.
